somnolence

SOM-nuh-lunss · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Somnolence is the formal word for the urge to fall asleep -- heavy eyelids and drifting attention.

A gentle somnolence settled over the passengers as the train rocked steadily through the night.

Example

The warm classroom and the teacher's droning voice combined to produce a heavy somnolence in the back row.

The heat and the droning voice together produced a specific feeling -- the urge to fall asleep -- which is exactly somnolence.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

drowsiness: the everyday word for feeling heavy-eyed and near sleep; somnolence is its formal, almost medical name

sleepiness: Sleepiness is the plain, everyday name for the urge to sleep. Somnolence means the very same urge -- the difference is register: somnolence is the formal, almost clinical term a doctor or a novelist might choose, while sleepiness belongs to ordinary conversation.

lethargy: Lethargy is a heavy lack of energy -- the whole body feels weighted, slow, and unwilling to move, whether or not sleep is calling. Somnolence is narrower: it names specifically the pull toward sleep itself, not a general shortage of energy.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

alertness: a state of being wide awake and attentive

Where it sits · how hard it is to stay awake — yawning → somnolence → stupor

yawning vs. somnolence: A single yawn is just a passing sign of tiredness; somnolence describes a heavier, more persistent pull toward sleep that settles over you.

stupor vs. somnolence: Somnolence still allows you to function, if sluggishly; a stupor is a near-unconscious daze you can barely think through.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — somn

root — somn: sleep (Latin (somnus))

suffix — -olence

suffix — -olence: having a tendency toward (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Somnolence comes from Latin somnus, 'sleep,' plus -olence, 'tending toward' -- so somnolence is literally a tendency toward sleep.
